findings.body: The `Calendar` interface changed `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent)` to `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent, credentialId: number)`. Only GoogleCalendarService was updated to accept and use `credentialId`. LarkCalendarService, Office365CalendarService, and BaseCalendarService (caldav/ical) still declare `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent)` with a single parameter. TypeScript structural typing permits implementations with fewer parameters, so this compiles, but the contract is now inconsistent: CalendarManager.createEvent always calls `calendar.createEvent(calEvent, credential.id)`, and any calendar service that needs to select a calendar per credential (as Google now does) cannot do so because the interface consumers other than Google ignore the second argument. More importantly, any external app implementing the old interface and relying on positional args is fine, but the interface no longer documents which implementations actually support per-credential selection. The interface and all implementations should be updated consistently (either all accept credentialId or the param should be optional).

findings.title: createEvent passes credential.id as the second argument, but the Calendar interface's second parameter is named/typed as credentialId while GoogleCalendarService matches destinationCalendar by credentialId — semantics mismatch with externalId usage in EventManager
findings.body: CalendarManager.createEvent calls `calendar.createEvent(calEvent, credential.id)` and also returns `externalId` (the third param passed from EventManager, which is `destination.externalId`). GoogleCalendarService.createEvent uses the second param (`credentialId`) to find the matching destination calendar: `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.credentialId === credentialId)`. This works only if `destinationCalendar` entries carry a `credentialId`. However, `DestinationCalendar` (the Prisma model) does NOT have a `credentialId` field — it has `integration`, `externalId`, `userId`/`eventTypeId`. The `credentialId` only exists on `IntegrationCalendar`/`SelectedCalendar`. So `cal.credentialId === credentialId` will be `undefined === number` → false for all entries, `selectedCalendar` will be undefined, and every Google event falls back to "primary" — silently defeating the entire purpose of the PR for Google Calendar. The matching key must be something present on DestinationCalendar (e.g. match by `integration` type against `credential.type`, or look up the credential's calendars).

findings.title: createAllCalendarEvents matches destination.credentialId against calendar credentials, but DestinationCalendar has no credentialId field
findings.body: In createAllCalendarEvents, the code checks `if (destination.credentialId)` and then finds the credential by `c.id === destination.credentialId`. The `destinationCalendar` array on CalendarEvent is typed as `DestinationCalendar[]` (Prisma model), which has no `credentialId` column (only `integration`, `externalId`, `userId`, `eventTypeId`, `eventTypeId`). Therefore `destination.credentialId` is always `undefined` at runtime, the `if` branch is never taken, and the code always falls into the `else` branch which matches by `destination.integration` against `credential.type`. This means: (a) the DB-fetch fallback for credentials not in the EventManager's list is dead code, and (b) for collective events where the organizer's EventManager only holds the organizer's credentials, other hosts' destination calendars (whose credentials are not in `this.calendarCredentials`) result in an empty `destinationCalendarCredentials` filter and NO event is created on the other hosts' calendars — the exact scenario the PR claims to fix. The credential resolution must be based on fields that actually exist (integration type + user/host), or the destination calendar entries must carry the credential id.

findings.title: Webhook e2e expectations for destinationCalendar are inconsistent (null vs []) and don't cover the new array shape
findings.body: The BOOKING_CREATED test still expects `destinationCalendar: null` (line 119) while the BOOKING_REJECTED test was changed to expect `destinationCalendar: []` (line 249), and BOOKING_REQUESTED still expects `null` (line 373). With the type change to `DestinationCalendar[] | null`, the webhook payload will now be an array (possibly empty) rather than null in most paths. The tests are inconsistent with each other and likely with actual behavior; at least one of them will fail or is already masking a regression. The expectations should be unified to the actual serialized value (likely `[]`) and ideally a collective-event webhook test should be added to verify multiple destination calendars are serialized.

findings.title: evt.destinationCalendar may be null when pushed to, causing a TypeError for collective events without any destination calendar
findings.body: The code sets `destinationCalendar: eventType.destinationCalendar ? [eventType.destinationCalendar] : organizerUser.destinationCalendar ? [organizerUser.destinationCalendar] : null` (line ~1063), then unconditionally does `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` (line 1075). The optional chaining protects against undefined, but if `evt.destinationCalendar` is `null` (the explicit `: null` branch), `null?.push(...)` evaluates to `undefined` without throwing — so no crash, but the team destination calendars are silently dropped when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar, even though team members do. The intent (fallback to normal behaviour but also support multiple) is not met in that case. The initial value should be `[]` instead of `null` so pushes always work.

findings.title: Lark createEvent now throws when destinationCalendar is empty, whereas before it fell back to the primary calendar
findings.body: Previously `const calendarId = event.destinationCalendar?.externalId;` yielded `undefined` when no destination calendar was set, and the code threw `new Error("no calendar id")` — so behavior is the same in the empty case. However, the new code `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? [];` combined with the existing `if (!calendarId) throw` means that for collective events where the FIRST destination calendar entry is not the one matching this credential (Lark's createEvent has no credentialId parameter to select among multiple destinations), the event is created on the first host's calendar only, and other hosts' Lark calendars never get the event. Since the Calendar interface now passes credentialId but Lark ignores it, multi-host Lark support is incomplete. At minimum this is a functional gap versus the PR's stated goal; the credentialId parameter should be used to select the matching destination calendar.

findings.title: BaseCalendarService (CalDAV/iCal) only creates the event on the first destination calendar, not on all hosts' calendars
findings.body: In BaseCalendarService.createEvent, `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and then the calendars list is filtered to only those matching `mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId` (or all calendars if none set). For a collective event with multiple hosts each having a CalDAV calendar, only the first host's calendar receives the event; the other hosts' calendars are filtered out. Since CalDAV credentials are per-user and the EventManager creates one BaseCalendarService per credential, the correct behavior would be to create the event on the calendar matching the current credential (like GoogleCalendarService attempts via credentialId), not just the first destination calendar entry. As written, collective events with multiple CalDAV hosts only block/create on one host's calendar.

findings.title: BrokenIntegrationEmail only reports the first destination calendar; multi-host breakage is misreported
findings.body: The email template takes `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = calEvent.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and builds the message from only that entry. For collective events where a non-first host's calendar integration is broken, the email will name the wrong calendar (the first host's) or fall back to the generic "calendar" string. This is a minor UX/reporting issue but misleading. The email should list all destination calendars or the specific failing one (the caller knows which credential failed).

findings.title: requestReschedule drops the user's destinationCalendar fallback that other handlers kept
findings.body: The original code was `destinationCalendar: bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar || bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar` (a no-op fallback to itself, clearly a pre-existing bug). The new code is `bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar ? [bookingToReschedule?.destinationCalendar] : []`, which removes even the (broken) intent and never falls back to the user's destination calendar, unlike confirm.handler.ts, editLocation.handler.ts, and handleCancelBooking.ts which all fall back to `user.destinationCalendar`. For bookings without a booking-level destination calendar, the webhook payload and any downstream calendar operations will see an empty array instead of the organizer's calendar. The fallback to the organizer's destination calendar should be restored for consistency.

findings.title: buildUIDCalendarEvent has an inverted guard that makes it always throw when users are set
findings.body: The method reads `if (this.users && this.users.length > 0) { throw new Error("call buildUsers before calling this function"); }` — the condition is inverted. It should throw when users are NOT set (`!this.users || this.users.length === 0`), because the very next lines destructure `const [mainOrganizer] = this.users;` and use `mainOrganizer.username`, which crashes on an empty array. As written, calling buildUIDCalendarEvent after buildUsers (the correct order) always throws, and calling it before buildUsers crashes on `mainOrganizer.username`. This is a pre-existing bug unrelated to the PR but it directly affects the reschedule-email builder path touched by this change (requestReschedule.handler.ts uses CalendarEventBuilder/Director).
